title: The Pros & Cons of Private Label Branding for CPG Brands
summary: Considering going private label with your CPG brand? Learn more about the pros & cons of this manufacturing model.
body_markdown:
[Manufacturing](https://thefreshfactory.co/blog-categories/manufacturing/) ,


[Tips](https://thefreshfactory.co/blog-categories/tips/)


August 25, 2026


The food industry chases[trends](https://thefreshfactory.co/blog/trends-expo-west-2026/) . As a co-manufacturer of better-for-you brands, The Fresh Factory sees a lot of innovation from our customers. But when a SKU gains popularity, it doesn’t stay solo in its category for long. Brands with successful CPGs often garner the interest of retailers that want a private label version on their shelves.


Whether a brand goes down the private label path depends on their strategy and needs. Saying yes gives the brand volume, shelf space, and a strong retailer relationship. But they have to sell at a discount and cede some control of a product they worked hard to build. On the other hand, exclusivity in food is hard to maintain. If the brand says no, the retailer will likely find someone else to reverse engineer and replicate the product.


Whether to accept private label business or remain branded is an age old question. Consider the following pros and cons to this[manufacturing model](https://thefreshfactory.co/blog/cpg-manufacturing-models/) .


## Advantages of Private Labeling Your Product


While store brands are already dominant abroad, their growth is on an upward trajectory in the U.S. According to the Private Label Manufacturers Association,[store brands outperformed national brands](https://www.plma.com/index%2ephp/article/store-brands-continue-gains-unit-sales-and-shares) for unit sales in the first half of 2026, rising to an all-time high of 23.8% market share. For food specifically, 52% of categories experienced private label growth.


Retailers and manufacturers are leaning into the private label category for good reason. Beyond the segment’s growth, here’s what makes it such a compelling strategy:


### Promotion Savings


Without the overhead of national advertising campaigns, brand-building budgets, or premium shelf placement fees, private label products typically cost less to bring to market. That savings shows up as pure production profit on the private label line, even if the per-unit price is lower than the brand’s own product.


### Increased Volume


Since the product formulation and production process already exist, taking on a private label version doesn’t require new[R&D](https://thefreshfactory.co/blog/research-development-phase/) , new equipment, or a new supply chain. This allows a brand to better utilize existing production capacity and generate more revenue from infrastructure that’s already in place.


### Brand Growth


While it may seem counterintuitive, a private label program does not necessarily inhibit a brand’s growth. While the shelf space allotted to private labels will likely remain consistent, new product introductions by the brand are still expected. And a strong retailer relationship may lead to more favorable terms and priority conversations for future opportunities.


### Economies of Scale


Running higher overall production volume can lower per-unit costs on materials, packaging, and freight. Those savings apply across the board, improving margins on the brand’s own products and the private label line.


## Private Label Disadvantages


Some retailers aren’t stopping at private label terms. They’re building the capacity to make the product themselves. In June 2025,[Walmart announced](https://corporate.walmart.com/news/2025/06/27/walmart-opens-first-owned-and-operated-case-ready-beef-facility-in-olathe-kansas) the grand opening of its first-ever owned and operated case-ready beef facility in Olathe, Kansas. The example serves as a reminder that a private label relationship isn’t guaranteed to last. A retailer that gains enough scale and confidence in a category can choose to bring production in-house. For a brand weighing whether to take on private label business, that risk is worth factoring in alongside these tradeoffs:


### Loss of Leverage


When you agree to a private label, you cede brand control. With a template for how to make your product and proven demand, there’s a risk that the retailer may eventually reduce its reliance on your brand, or replace it.


### Operational Challenges


Retailers often use private label programs to differentiate themselves from competitors, frequently requesting unique adjustments to product formulas and packaging. This can create additional SKUs for the manufacturer, leading to production and floor stock issues as well as supply chain inefficiencies.


### Margin Compression


Private label pricing is typically negotiated at a discount to the brand’s own retail price. That means the volume gained through a private label agreement often comes at a lower per-unit margin, a tradeoff that needs to pencil out against the added production efficiency it brings.


### Reduced Brand Visibility


Every unit produced under a retailer’s label is a unit that isn’t building recognition for the brand itself. Over time, heavy reliance on private label volume can mean a brand’s own name carries less weight with consumers.


## The Best of Both Worlds


Saying yes to a private label doesn’t have to mean choosing between a brand’s own line and a retailer’s version of it. Many stores run both side by side, letting the branded product and its private label counterpart coexist on the same shelf. Some retailer partnerships go a step further with co-labeling, featuring both the retailer’s name and the original brand’s on the same package.


## Scaling Production


Weighing whether to take on private label business comes down to strategy, capacity, and how much control a brand is willing to share in exchange for volume and retailer trust.


**Our recommendation:** Take the business. “Exclusivity, especially in food, is very difficult,” says Bill Besenhofer, CEO and co-founder of The Fresh Factory. “You can always reverse engineer food, especially clean food. Of course it depends on your brand and goals, but taking the business is often better than risking someone else taking it and surpassing you.”


If your brand is weighing a private label opportunity, The Fresh Factory can help you scale production to meet it, without sacrificing the quality or consistency your customers expect from your own line.
